content: Structured antenatal education programs are frequently recommended by healthcare professionals worldwide for pregnant women and their partners. These programs are designed to provide education about childbirth, parenthood, or both, and are typically delivered in group settings, though they may also be offered individually. The objective of this review was to evaluate the impact of antenatal education on various outcomes, including knowledge acquisition, anxiety levels, sense of control, pain management, labor and birth support, breastfeeding success, infant-care skills, and psychological and social adjustment. To gather relevant studies, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register, CINAHL, ERIC, EMBASE, and PsycINFO, covering publications up to April 2006. Additional handsearching of the Journal of Psychosomatic Research (1956 to April 2006) and reference lists of retrieved studies was performed. The search was later updated in July 2011, with new findings added to the awaiting classification section. The review included randomized controlled trials of structured educational programs provided during pregnancy by an educator to either parent. These programs addressed topics related to pregnancy, childbirth, or parenthood and could be delivered individually or in groups. However, studies focusing exclusively on breastfeeding success, postpartum depression, maternal psychosocial health (e.g., anxiety, depression, self-esteem), or smoking cessation were excluded. Two authors independently assessed the quality of the trials and extracted data from the published reports. Ultimately, nine trials involving a total of 2,284 women were included in the review, while 37 studies were excluded. Of the included trials, eight focused on educational interventions, with a combined sample size of 1,009 participants. However, details regarding randomization procedures, allocation concealment, and participant accrual or loss were not consistently reported across these studies. The sample sizes ranged from very small (10 participants) to moderate (318 participants). The review found no consistent results across the included studies. Data on anxiety, breastfeeding success, and general social support were not reported. Outcomes such as knowledge acquisition, sense of control, infant-care competencies, and some labor and birth outcomes were measured. The largest study included in the review (n = 1,275) investigated an educational and social support intervention aimed at increasing vaginal birth rates after cesarean section. This high-quality study found no significant difference in vaginal birth rates between groups receiving verbal education and those receiving document-based education (relative risk 1.08, 95% confidence interval 0.97 to 1.21). The authors concluded that the overall effects of general antenatal education for childbirth or parenthood remain largely unknown. Furthermore, individualized prenatal education aimed at reducing repeat cesarean births does not appear to increase the rate of vaginal birth after cesarean section. It is noted that the 58 citations in the awaiting classification section may influence the conclusions of this review once they are assessed.
